Zedonk is genuinely best for small and mid-size fashion brands that need sales, production, inventory and wholesale in one system built around size curves, seasons and linesheets. Skip it if you are not a fashion business — this is deliberately niche — or you want self-serve, monthly-cancellable software rather than an annual, demo-led ERP.

Modular fashion-ERP, priced per building block and billed annually, all listed as 'prices starting from': PLM £166/mo, ERP Essential £166/mo, B2C (adds Shopify integration and barcodes) £250/mo, B2B (adds the digital wholesale showroom) £332/mo. No self-serve signup — every tier goes through a demo, and the real price depends on which modules you stack. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Zedonk?
answers.a: The 'starting from' wording is doing real work: £166/mo is the floor of the cheapest module, billed annually, so a working setup for a brand that sells wholesale quickly stacks toward £332/mo and beyond — about £4,000 a year before add-ons. There is no trial and no public total: you find out your actual price in a demo call. Budget for the stack, not the sticker.

Zeffy is genuinely best for small and mid-size nonprofits that want donations, ticketing, memberships and payments without any fee eating the mission's money. Skip it if your organization objects to donor-facing tip prompts on principle, or you need enterprise CRM-grade donor management built in.

Genuinely $0 for nonprofits (2026): no platform, transaction or card-processing fees on donations, ticketing or payments. The model: donors see an optional (zero-able) tip prompt at checkout, and enough tip to fund the platform. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Zeffy?
answers.a: The honest scrutiny of 'free': the tip prompt is shown to YOUR donors, with suggested percentages — most give happily, but some organizations feel it inserts a step between donor and cause, and a donor who tips 10% effectively paid a fee, just voluntarily and not from your share. Compare that trade against the 2-5% the paid platforms take from every donation, and for most small nonprofits the math strongly favors Zeffy.

ZenBusiness is genuinely best for first-time founders who want the paperwork handled and are willing to pay a yearly fee to keep it handled — the a-la-carte pricing means you can start at the state fee plus a registered agent and add only what you actually need. Skip it if you are comfortable filing with your state yourself and acting as your own registered agent, in which case the state fee is the only unavoidable cost and the $199/year is buying convenience and a business address rather than anything you cannot do; or you need legal advice rather than filing, since a formation service is not a law firm.

(2026-07-25, read on their own pricing page) Formation itself is $0 plus the state's fee — that applies to LLC, S corp and C corp filings alike, and the state fee is separate, varies by state and is not shown until you pick one. Everything else is priced as its own line rather than bundled into plan tiers. The recurring items are registered agent at $199/year, Worry-Free Compliance Filing at $199/year, and Advanced Compliance Protection at $299/year. One-time filings: operating agreement $99, EIN $99, business document templates $99, rush filing $79, DBA registration $95 plus state fees, business licence report $149, amendment $100, certificate of good standing $100, annual report filing $100 per report, and New York publication $200 for the state that requires it. There is a second catalogue alongside the legal one: business website $129/year, eCommerce website $279/year, domain $25/year, domain privacy $10/year, logo kit $60, business banking $5/month and Money Pro with online payments $30/month. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with ZenBusiness?
answers.a: The $0 is real for the filing service and it is also the whole commercial idea: what you sign up for at zero has an annual carry that is not shown next to it. A registered agent is a legal requirement in every state, and theirs is $199/year — so the realistic first-year cost of 'the $0 LLC' is the state fee plus $199, before compliance filing at another $199/year. Price the second year, not the first. The second thing to hold in view is that the state fee is the largest and most variable number in the whole exercise and ZenBusiness cannot change it: it is set by your state, ranges widely, and their own page sends you to a lookup rather than quoting it. Anyone comparing formation services on the advertised price alone is comparing the small half of the bill.

ZenZap is genuinely best for small teams that run work over messy WhatsApp/personal chat today and want organized, professional chat with tasks — starting free. Skip it if your workflows depend on a deep integration ecosystem (Slack's moat), or you're already paid into Microsoft Teams via 365.

Free plan with unlimited users, chats and built-in to-dos; Pro about $3/user/mo (integrations, storage); Business+ ~$8/user/mo (roles, audit trails, SLAs); Enterprise custom. Annual billing prices best. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with ZenZap?
answers.a: The pricing genuinely undercuts Slack — the honest question is ecosystem: team chat lives or dies on integrations and habit, and ZenZap's app catalog is a fraction of Slack's, so teams glued to hundreds of integrations will feel the gap. For WhatsApp-refugee teams that mainly need organized channels, tasks and work/life separation, the free tier is a remarkably complete landing spot.

ZoomInfo is genuinely best for enterprise go-to-market teams that need the deepest US database, buyer-intent signals and conversation intelligence — and can absorb the contract. Skip it if you're an SMB or want flexible month-to-month pricing — the cost, credit burn and lock-in rarely pay off below enterprise scale.

Sales-gated — no public rates, no monthly billing and no free plan. Contracts typically start around $15k and the median runs near ~$32k/yr, climbing once seats, credits and add-ons (intent, international data) stack up (2026). Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with ZoomInfo?
answers.a: The contract is the most-cited frustration: annual lock-in with a strict 60–90 day cancellation window and 10–20% renewal increases. Credits burn fast, data can be stale (prospects who left years ago), and it's built for enterprise — overkill and overpriced for SMBs, with weaker accuracy outside the US.

doola is genuinely best for founders (often non-US) who want US LLC/C-Corp formation, EIN and compliance handled in one place without the paperwork. Skip it if you're a US resident comfortable filing formation yourself — the state fee plus a cheap registered agent costs far less than the bundle.

Starter about $297/yr (LLC or C-Corp formation, EIN, registered agent, US address); Pulse bookkeeping ~$300/yr; Tax and Compliance ~$1,999/yr; Business-in-a-Box ~$2,999/yr — plus state filing fees on top ($50-500 by state) (2026). Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with doola?
answers.a: Formation is the cheap part; the recurring bookkeeping and tax tiers are where the real cost sits, and state fees are extra on top of doola's price. Convenient especially for non-US founders, but a local accountant may be cheaper once you're established.

eDesk is genuinely best for e-commerce and marketplace sellers who want one unified inbox across Amazon, eBay, Shopify and email — with order data and AI-assisted replies where support and revenue overlap. Skip it if you run a non-commerce SaaS or service business (general helpdesks fit better and cheaper), or your ticket volume is low enough that a shared inbox already copes.

(verified 17 Jul 2026) Free plan to start; Essential $39/agent/mo, Growth $89/agent/mo (Recommended), Professional $119/agent/mo, Enterprise custom — all billed annually (20% off vs monthly). The AI Agent is included on paid tiers but its automated resolutions bill separately at $0.99 per outcome — you only pay when it actually resolves a query, not per attempt. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with eDesk?
answers.a: Two meters, and the second one is easy to miss: the per-agent price is the entry ticket, but the AI Agent charges $0.99 for every automated resolution on top — great when it deflects real tickets, but a variable line item that scales with your support volume, so model it against your ticket count before assuming a flat bill. And the honest fundamental for any e-commerce helpdesk: the value is only as good as your marketplace integrations actually syncing — test Amazon/eBay/Shopify connections with your real accounts during the free trial.

folk is genuinely best for small sales teams, agencies and VC/partnership teams who want a clean, fast-to-set-up CRM with a great LinkedIn enrichment extension. Skip it if you're a solo founder who needs your network on your phone, or you need real workflow automation and reporting — folk is lightweight by design.
$20/user/mo (Standard), $40 (Premium), Custom from $80; ~20% off annual, 14-day free trial, no card (2026). Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with folk?
answers.a: Two real gaps: there's no mobile app (browser only — the #1 complaint), and no proper workflow automation on any plan, just trigger-based emails. Enrichment is capped (~500–1,000/mo) and email sequences need at least Premium.

iContact is genuinely best for small businesses and nonprofits who want a simple, reliable email tool with strong deliverability and a real marketing advisor included on every paid plan. Skip it if you need advanced multi-branch automation (ActiveCampaign does more) or you're chasing the rock-bottom cheapest option.

No permanent free plan any more — a 30-day free trial, then paid tiers by contact count: at 500 contacts, Standard $9/mo (templates, landing pages, automations) and Premium $16/mo (unlimited users, social posting, AI content assistant), plus custom for large lists. Pay yearly to save 15% (re-verified 2026-07-19). Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with iContact?
answers.a: Pricing feels a touch high for what you get, and the Standard plan's hard caps on automations and landing pages push growing teams to upgrade sooner than expected. It's also less cutting-edge on automation than ActiveCampaign — its real edge is simplicity, strong deliverability and the included human support.

involve.me is genuinely best for marketers building interactive lead-gen — quizzes, calculators, assessments and payment funnels with built-in email sequences — who want a free tier to validate the concept first. Skip it if you just need a simple form (lighter tools do that free), or you don’t yet have the traffic to feed an interactive funnel.

(verified 17 Jul 2026) Free tier to start; Start $19/mo billed annually ($29 month-to-month) with 3 live funnels and 1 user; Grow $49/mo annual ($69 monthly) with 5 funnels and 2 users; Scale $119/mo annual ($139 monthly) with 25 funnels, A/B testing and lead verification; Enterprise from $399/mo on annual contracts only. Extra seats $10/user/mo. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with involve.me?
answers.a: The tier ladder is really a funnel-count ladder — 3 live funnels on Start evaporates once you run campaigns in parallel, and the advertised prices are annual: month-to-month runs $10-20 higher per tier. And the honest fundamental for any interactive-funnel tool: quizzes and calculators convert traffic you already have — they don’t create it, so validate on the free tier before the subscription outruns the pipeline.

lemlist is genuinely best for outbound teams that live in cold email and want multichannel sequences, warm-up and a big template community in one per-seat tool. Skip it if you send occasional one-off campaigns — per-seat pricing from ~$39/user only pays off with steady outbound volume.
No free plan; paid runs roughly $39/user/mo (Email Starter) up to ~$159/user/mo (Outreach Scale) as of 2026. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with lemlist?
answers.a: The per-seat plus per-email-account model makes total cost unpredictable as you scale, and reviews flag support response times and the LinkedIn Chrome-extension's reliability.
